purpose: Structural benchmark corpus for Oxford-like problem authoring without reproducing source questions.
copyright_policy: Store source references and abstract structural summaries only. Do not copy full problem statements, full transcripts, or solution prose.

evidence_labels.official-sample: University/department publishes the item specifically as a sample interview question.
evidence_labels.actual-used: First-party source says the problem or an adapted version was used in an Oxford interview.
evidence_labels.interview-style-extension: Oxford preparation material explicitly says an item/extension could or has been used to begin an interview.
evidence_labels.subject-adjacent-actual-used: Actual Oxford Maths/CS or CS interview evidence; useful but not treated as pure Maths frequency evidence.

benchmarks.opening_style: Concrete visual motion with an intuitive prediction before formal modelling.

progression.summary: Predict and/or sketch the locus traced by a marked point during a constrained motion.
Draw several positions and form a hypothesis.
Replace the sketch with variables and a geometric constraint.
Use the invariant geometric relation to characterize the locus.
Move the marked point away from the midpoint and determine how the locus changes.

tutor_interventions: Ask how the candidate could test an initially visual hypothesis.
If stuck, direct attention to the geometric shape formed at every position rather than giving the locus.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Makes abstraction and modelling visible; an intuitive answer can be checked and corrected mathematically.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: physical motion -> geometric constraint -> algebraic locus -> parameterized family
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor commentary explicitly emphasizes abstraction, modelling, testing a hypothesis, and generalising beyond an inaccurate sketch.

benchmarks.opening_style: Low-prerequisite enumeration of the first few small cases.

progression.summary: Draw/count cases for the first few sizes.
Explain systematically why a listed case count has no omissions.
Use additional values to identify a recurrence-like pattern; knowing its conventional name is irrelevant.
Explain structurally why the recurrence occurs.
Change grid dimension and tile shape, then reuse or revise the learned decomposition.

tutor_interventions: Explicitly reassure that an immediate answer is not expected and suggest small cases.
Provide later numerical values to expose a pattern when useful.
Continue giving hints in the modified problem while testing whether earlier ideas were absorbed.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Very low knowledge burden with a high ceiling and repeated opportunities to show learning.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: finite examples -> recurrence -> structural decomposition -> altered combinatorial system
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor explicitly says the knowledge content is no more than GCSE while the internal complexity can test very strong candidates.

source.provenance_note: Oxford states this is adapted from a question James Munro used for Maths interviews.

benchmarks.opening_style: Sketch a simple parameterised function using qualitative behavior before deep calculation.

progression.summary: Describe small/large-input behavior and locate the turning point of a parameterised curve.
Reason qualitatively about composing the function without expanding everything.
Iterate the map and predict the long-run behavior.
Prove a quantitative local bound and interpret the speed of convergence.

tutor_interventions: Prompt with asymptotic behavior at small and large inputs.
Ask for qualitative composition reasoning before algebraic substitution.
Escalate to a quantitative bound only if the interview supports it.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Combines school-level technique with genuine mathematical thinking, iteration, and a very high ceiling.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: graph features -> function composition -> dynamical iteration -> local quantitative estimate
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The official solution explicitly makes the final quantitative proof contingent on how the interview is going.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Only structural description stored; formula omitted from this corpus.

benchmarks.opening_style: Classify feasible small sizes for a geometric tiling construction.

progression.summary: Try small values and draw explicit constructions.
Strengthen an informal impossibility claim by focusing on local/corner structure.
Recognize operations that generate further feasible sizes.
Combine impossibility reasoning and constructions into a broader description.

tutor_interventions: Redirect a weak impossibility argument to a more local geometric feature.
Ask targeted questions about corners/rectangle placement.
Use earlier constructions to prompt a reusable growth rule.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Shows real-time recovery from mistakes and how tutor input can reveal, rather than replace, a candidate's thinking.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: small constructions -> local obstruction -> generative construction -> classification
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Post-interview tutor commentary emphasizes thought process, creativity, pattern spotting, persistence, and use of a newly noticed construction.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No transcript or full statement reproduced.

source.caveat: Use for structural evidence, not pure Mathematics topic-frequency estimates.

benchmarks.opening_style: Constrained selection problem where small cases expose interaction between two rules.

progression.summary: Test small admissible values and try a simple selection strategy.
Pair complementary objects so one global constraint becomes local.
Notice when the forbidden-object condition interacts with the pairing rule.
Change the power/forbidden class and determine what carries over.
If time remains, count the valid selections rather than only decide existence.

tutor_interventions: Suggest small cases early if the candidate does not.
Help isolate the interaction of the two constraints rather than naming a theorem.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Tests whether a candidate can connect two elementary areas without being told the connection.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: examples -> complementary pairing -> hidden interaction -> altered exponent/class
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor explicitly says complete polished solutions are not the point and that small cases may be prompted.

source.caveat: Use for structural evidence, not pure Mathematics topic-frequency estimates.

benchmarks.opening_style: Concrete digit manipulation admits an algorithmic trial approach before formalization.

progression.summary: Run a familiar digit-by-digit procedure to generate information.
Notice that a small state determines the next state.
Use finite-state repetition/uniqueness to justify why the procedure eventually cycles or terminates as claimed.
Encode the digit movement as an algebraic equation.
Replace the digit and multiplier with parameters and ask when the construction exists.

tutor_interventions: Encourage starting the mechanical process rather than waiting for a closed form.
Prompt the candidate to identify what information determines the next step.
Accept either procedural or algebraic routes and compare them.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Creates multiple viable representations and lets the candidate develop an algorithm into a proof.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: concrete process -> state machine -> finiteness argument -> algebraic encoding -> parameterized family
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor commentary says the subtle full proof was not expected without help and values the mathematical reasoning about the procedure.

source.provenance_note: The author explicitly describes how the underlying item could begin an interview.

benchmarks.opening_style: Begin from an elementary symmetry/area observation in a familiar regular shape.

progression.summary: Identify an area-bisecting line in a symmetric figure.
Ask whether the same centre/bisection relationship holds for other regular polygons.
Make the meaning of 'centre' precise enough for the discussion.
Separate a sufficient-looking symmetry observation from what is actually proved.
Search for other shapes where centre lines bisect area and test converses.

tutor_interventions: Avoid detailed area calculation and focus on symmetry/definition.
Ask whether the observed property is sufficient or merely suggestive.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Turns an easy-looking geometry fact into a proof/definition/generalization discussion.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: familiar symmetry -> generalized claim -> define centre -> test sufficiency/converse
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Official preparation material explicitly frames this as an interview continuation.

benchmarks.opening_style: A geometric relation is derived first; its algebraic meaning is then extracted.

progression.summary: Establish a length relation in a simple circle configuration.
Recognize the relation as a general inequality between positive quantities.
Use the geometry to justify the inequality.
Apply it to reciprocal expressions or fixed-perimeter optimization.

tutor_interventions: Keep the geometric interpretation active rather than immediately naming the inequality.
After deriving it, ask for applications in algebra/optimization.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Strong example of learning a tool inside the interview and immediately transferring it.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: geometric identity -> inequality -> algebraic applications -> optimization
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Official material explicitly suggests this kind of extension as an interview continuation.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No source formulas or full problem text stored.

benchmarks.opening_style: Interpret a two-variable equation geometrically instead of solving point-by-point.

progression.summary: Replace an expression in x and y by a radial variable.
Interpret allowed radial values as families of concentric curves.
Reason about spacing as a nonlinear transformation changes.
Change the outer function and predict the new radial graph family.

tutor_interventions: Suggest thinking in terms of radius rather than separate coordinates.
Ask how a nonlinear square-root map changes equal spacings.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Demonstrates that graph sketching can test structure and representation rather than routine plotting.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: two-variable equation -> radius parameter -> family of level sets -> changed outer function
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Official solutions explicitly describe a related graph as a possible next interview question.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No full equation or answer choices stored.
